findings.claim: Across all seven lessons, all 42 practice questions are labelled “40 marks — Post-1914 Essay” but carry a 20-mark band ladder (“Top band (17-20)” ... “Lower band (1-4)”), and 14 of them carry a 12-mark ladder (“Top band (11-12)” ... “Lower band (1-2)”). Band names repeat “Top band” twice and use “Lower band”, which is not the house ladder. L1 Q1 also credits alternative interpretations to AO4.
findings.truth: The Edexcel post-1914 play essay is one question from a choice of two, worth 40 marks: AO1 and AO3 are marked together out of 32 on a five-level grid (1-6, 7-12, 13-19, 20-26, 27-32) and AO4 adds 8 marks for accurate written expression. Pearson's own exemplar scripts for The Empress are marked "AO1/3 Level 3 (18 marks)" and "AO1/3 Level 4 (25 marks)" with "AO4 Level 3 (6/8 marks)".
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 1 overview and raw-mark table (Questions 7 to 30: AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8 = 40); Pearson 'The Empress' Exemplar Scripts and Commentaries (March 2021), question stem 'Total for Question 15 = 40 marks (includes 8 marks for the range of appropriate vocabulary and sentence structures, and accurate use of spelling and punctuation)'.

findings.claim: A character called "Mrs Phelps" is taught across five lessons as "the play's most prominent British character", the employer who abandons the ayahs, and the embodiment of Victorian racism. She appears 30 times: in content, a glossary term, knowledge-check keys, flashcards, practice questions and L5's lesson description.
findings.truth: There is no Mrs Phelps in The Empress. The British employer who hires Rani as an ayah and dismisses her the moment the ship docks is Susan Matthews ("No written contract you understand... It is not legally binding"; "You are merely my servant's offspring"). The court racist is Lady Sarah, Victoria's lady-in-waiting. The most prominent British character is Queen Victoria herself. All 30 mentions changed to Susan Matthews, and the "most prominent British character" claim dropped.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character list for The Empress (Rani Das, Hari Sharma, Abdul Karim, Queen Victoria, Lady Sarah, Dadhabai Naoroji, Lascar Sally, Firoza, Gandhi, Cecil Rhodes, Albert, Susan Matthews, Lord Oakham, Georgie, Serang Ali, Mary, Charlotte, William, Asha) https://www.litcharts.com/lit/the-empress/characters ; Pearson exemplar scripts name "Mr and Mrs Matthews" as the employers.

findings.claim: "Queen Victoria never appears on stage in The Empress" (L1); "Gupta's choice to keep Victoria offstage is deliberate" (L1); L5's collapsible "Queen Victoria — The Absent Centre" says in one paragraph both that she "appears on stage throughout the play as a significant speaking character" and that "Gupta's decision to keep Victoria offstage is a deliberate structural choice"; L6 lists "Queen Victoria as an offstage presence". A knowledge check, three flashcards and a practice question all key on her absence.
findings.truth: Queen Victoria is a major speaking role. Half the play is her court: Abdul Karim is sent to her as a Golden Jubilee gift in 1887, teaches her Hindi, becomes her Munshi, and Lady Sarah works to remove him. Pearson's own exemplar script describes her being "introduced in Windsor Castle, eating an egg from a golden egg cup". The L5 paragraph contradicted itself, so a previous partial repair had been left half-finished.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, The Empress (play) plot and cast; LitCharts character analysis (Queen Victoria, Lady Sarah); Pearson 'The Empress' Exemplar Scripts and Commentaries, Script 2.

findings.claim: "The real Ayahs' Home was established in Hackney, East London, by the London City Mission" (L1), repeated in the L4 glossary and dfn definition and in two flashcards as "Hackney ... opened in 1891".
findings.truth: The Home was at 6 Jewry Street, Aldgate in 1891. It moved to 26 King Edward's Road, Hackney only in 1900, and to 4 King Edward's Road in 1921. The London City Mission did run it. The 1891 date is kept; the location is corrected to Aldgate with the Hackney move dated 1900.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Ayahs' Home; Making Britain (Open University), Ayahs' Home; English Heritage blue plaque page for the Ayahs' Home.

findings.claim: The play is "set it in the 1880s–1890s" (content), "set during the height of the British Empire in the 1880s–1890s" (conclusion), "The 1880s–1890s" (flashcard).
findings.truth: The play runs from the 1887 Golden Jubilee to Victoria's death in 1901, so it covers the 1897 Diamond Jubilee and the reign's end. Corrected to 1887 to 1901.
findings.evidence: LitCharts key facts, setting: 'Various locations in London, from 1887 to 1901'.

findings.claim: "This authorial intent is directly relevant to AO3."
findings.truth: The house validator rejects an AO code immediately followed by a full stop. Rewritten as "...relevant to AO3 (context)."

findings.claim: Banned strings in lesson fields: "For Edexcel Component 1 Section B" (L1 exam tip), "common in Edexcel Component 1" (L6 exam tip), "strengthens an Edexcel essay at Level 5" (L7 flashcard).
findings.truth: The house validator rejects "Component 1", "Paper N Section X" codes and "Level 1"-"Level 9" band names anywhere in a lesson field. Replaced with "the Edexcel post-1914 play essay" and "in the top band".

findings.claim: AO4 is taught throughout the unit as evaluation and alternative interpretations: "For Edexcel AO4, you must evaluate different interpretations" (L4), "Act 2 is rich material for AO4 (evaluation)" (L3), "For AO4, consider alternative interpretations" (L2), "allowing the audience to evaluate them through AO4" (L5), "always offer alternative interpretations for AO4" (L7 conclusion), plus AO4 credits inside mark schemes. That is the AQA reading of AO4 carried over to Edexcel.
findings.truth: On Edexcel 1ET0 the post-1914 essay assesses AO1, AO3 and AO4, and AO4 is the 8 marks for a range of appropriate vocabulary and sentence structures with accurate spelling and punctuation. Evaluation and alternative readings are credited under AO1 (critical style and informed personal response). Every AO4 claim rewritten; the SPaG marks now stated instead.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md Component 1 overview ('Marks will also be given for accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar'; 'Assessment Objectives covered are AO1, AO3 and AO4') and the raw-mark table; Pearson exemplar commentaries mark AO4 on spelling slips only.

findings.claim: L2 flashcard: "Who is Rani's husband travelling with her to London?" answer "Abdul." L5 flashcard: "Who is Abdul in The Empress?" answer "Rani's husband — representing quiet strength and pragmatic survival within a hostile system."
findings.truth: Abdul Karim is a real historical figure with a separate storyline: he is sent to Queen Victoria as a Golden Jubilee gift and becomes her Munshi. Rani's romantic partner is Hari Sharma, the lascar. The L5 content body already carries a correction note saying exactly this, so the flashcards contradict their own lesson.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character analysis, Abdul Karim and Hari Sharma; Wikipedia, The Empress (play).

findings.claim: "What common promise did Indian employers break to the ayahs?"
findings.truth: The employers who hired ayahs for the voyage and then abandoned them were British families, as the lesson body states. Corrected to "British employers".
findings.evidence: L2 content_html, same lesson; Making Britain, Ayahs' Home.

findings.claim: "By the 1880s, lascars made up around a quarter of the British merchant navy", repeated as a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: Lascar numbers rose across the period and peaked at 17.5 per cent of British merchant crews (about 51,000 men) in 1914, so a quarter in the 1880s is not credible. The safe sourced figure is that some 24,000 lascars were employed in the British merchant navy in the early 1890s. The 'one-fifth of a white sailor's wage' claim in the same paragraph is within the range sources give (one-fifth to one-quarter) and is left alone.
findings.evidence: Our Migration Story, 'The lascars: Britain's colonial sailors'; South Asian Britain, 'Lascars'; 1914-1918-Online, 'Lascar'.

findings.claim: "Naoroji won by a margin of just three votes", and the flashcard answer "Three votes".
findings.truth: Naoroji beat the sitting member F. T. Penton by 2,961 to 2,956 in Central Finsbury on 6 July 1892 — a majority of five, which earned him the nickname 'Mr Narrow Majority'.
findings.evidence: Journal of Liberal History, 'Dadabhai Naoroji, 1825-1917'; Our Migration Story, 'The first Indian MP: Dadabhai Naoroji'.

findings.claim: Flashcard: "How did Lord Salisbury racially dismiss Naoroji?" answer "By mockingly calling him 'a black man' and questioning whether a 'fire-worshipper' could represent British voters."
findings.truth: The same lesson's content body states that 'fire-worshipper' was used by hostile campaign opponents and is not Salisbury's, and that students should attribute only 'a black man' to him. Salisbury's Edinburgh speech of 1888 said he doubted a British constituency would elect 'a black man'. The flashcard was left behind by an earlier repair to the body text.
findings.evidence: L4 content_html, same lesson; Salisbury, Edinburgh, 30 November 1888.

findings.claim: "Abdul demonstrates quiet strength — enduring hardship while protecting those around him" and "Abdul's pragmatism keeps him and Rani alive, but it does not change the system."
findings.truth: Abdul Karim lives at Windsor as the Queen's Munshi. He endures the court's hostility, chiefly from Lady Sarah, not hardship at the docks, and he has no part in keeping Rani alive — their storylines are separate, as this lesson states three paragraphs earlier. Rani is helped by Lascar Sally, Firoza and the Home for Ayahs.
findings.evidence: LitCharts plot summary and character analysis, Abdul Karim, Lady Sarah, Lascar Sally, Firoza.

findings.claim: "For the Edexcel exam, you are assessed on your ability to analyse how a playwright uses language, form, and structure to create meaning (AO1)."
findings.truth: That sentence is the wording of AO2, and AO2 is not assessed on the post-1914 play question. The objectives here are AO1 (critical style and informed personal response supported by references), AO3 (context) and AO4 (written expression). Analysing form and structure still earns credit, but through AO1.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md Component 1: 'Section B ... Assessment Objectives covered are AO1, AO3 and AO4'.

findings.claim: A whole section teaches that "Gupta structures the play across a dual timeline, moving between different periods in the 1880s and 1890s" and that "when the audience sees characters in the earlier timeline making hopeful plans, they already know (from scenes set later) how those plans will be thwarted". Repeated in the lesson description, a key fact, a glossary term, a knowledge check pair, two flashcards and a practice question.
findings.truth: The Empress runs forward in time from 1887 to 1901 in two acts of fifteen scenes. There is no second time period and no flash-forward. What Gupta does use is two parallel storylines — Rani at the docks and Victoria's court — cut against each other. All references changed to parallel storylines.
findings.evidence: LitCharts key facts and structure (2 acts, 15 scenes each; setting 'from 1887 to 1901'); LitCharts plot summary.

findings.claim: "blending real historical figures (Dadabhai Naoroji, Queen Victoria as an offstage presence) with fictional characters (Rani, Abdul, Hari)".
findings.truth: Abdul Karim is a real historical figure — L1 of this same unit says so. The real figures in the play include Naoroji, Queen Victoria, Abdul Karim, Gandhi and Cecil Rhodes. Rani, Hari and Firoza are the invented ones.
findings.evidence: L1 content_html, same unit; LitCharts character analysis; Wikipedia, Abdul Karim (the Munshi).

findings.claim: Lessons 2, 3 and 4 are titled and written as "Act 1", "Act 2" and "Act 3". L4 opens "Act 3 of The Empress brings the play to its resolution" and its knowledge check asks students to "Match each Act 3 event to what it represents". L3 places the ayahs' abandonment in Act 2.
findings.truth: The Empress has TWO acts of fifteen scenes each. There is no Act 3, and Rani's dismissal by Susan Matthews happens early in Act 1, not in Act 2, so no one lesson covers a whole act. Every in-body reference is now act-neutral: lesson 2 uses 'the opening scenes', lesson 3 'the middle of the play' or 'these scenes', lesson 4 'the final scenes' or 'the closing scenes'. Section headings become 'Arrival:', 'Exploitation:' and 'Resolution:'. Lesson 6 now states the real structure - two acts of fifteen scenes each. Lesson titles are excluded from these edits; the coordinator is dropping the 'Act N:' prefix separately.
findings.evidence: LitCharts study guide, structure: 2 acts, 15 scenes each; LitCharts plot summary (Rani fired by Susan Matthews on arrival, 1887).

summary: Seven lessons, eighteen findings (11 HIGH, 5 MEDIUM, 2 LOW), all fixed; 187 surgical edits written. The unit invents a character (Mrs Phelps), denies that Queen Victoria appears on stage, presents the play as three acts when it has two, teaches AQA's AO4 instead of Edexcel's written-expression objective, and puts a 20-mark ladder under every 40-mark essay.
